claim: The frontal pole (FP) is involved in metacognition.
source: We focused on two well-known cognitive operations, both considered as executive functions, and involving distinct regions of the prefrontal cortex: metacognition, which involves the frontal pole (FP), and working memory, which involves the dorso-lateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC), as demonstrated by extensive work in humans and macaques (Fuster, 2008; Mansouri et al., 2017; Passingham et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature (Fuster, 2008; Mansouri et al., 2017; Passingham et al., 2012) demonstrating the relationship between FP and metacognition.

claim: The dorso-lateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) is involved in working memory.
source: We focused on two well-known cognitive operations, both considered as executive functions, and involving distinct regions of the prefrontal cortex: metacognition, which involves the frontal pole (FP), and working memory, which involves the dorso-lateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC), as demonstrated by extensive work in humans and macaques (Fuster, 2008; Mansouri et al., 2017; Passingham et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature (Fuster, 2008; Mansouri et al., 2017; Passingham et al., 2012) demonstrating the relationship between DLPFC and working memory.

claim: The size of the whole brain, frontal pole, and dorso-lateral prefrontal cortex was best explained by body mass, daily traveled distance, and population density.
source: The size of these prefrontal regions, as well as the whole brain, was best explained by three variables: body mass, daily traveled distance (an index of ecological constraints), and population density (an index of social constraints).
evidence: This is the main finding from the model comparison approach using phylogenetic generalized least squares (PGLS) analysis conducted in the study.

claim: Daily traveled distance is an index of ecological constraints.
source: The size of these prefrontal regions, as well as the whole brain, was best explained by three variables: body mass, daily traveled distance (an index of ecological constraints), and population density (an index of social constraints).
evidence: The authors explicitly define daily traveled distance as representing ecological constraints in their study design.

claim: Population density is an index of social constraints.
source: The size of these prefrontal regions, as well as the whole brain, was best explained by three variables: body mass, daily traveled distance (an index of ecological constraints), and population density (an index of social constraints).
evidence: The authors explicitly define population density as representing social constraints in their study design.

claim: FP volume was much more sensitive to social constraints than DLPFC volume.
source: Interestingly, FP volume was much more sensitive to social constraints than DLPFC volume, in line with laboratory studies showing an implication of FP in complex social interactions.
evidence: This is a key finding from the comparative analysis of how population density (social constraints) affects FP versus DLPFC volumes.

claim: The social brain hypothesis proposes that social interactions played a central role in the increase in brain size during primate evolution.
source: One of the major hypotheses, referred to as the 'social brain' hypothesis, proposes that social interactions require higher cognitive skills such that the complexity of social interactions played a central role in the increase in brain size during primate evolution (Dunbar, 1998).
evidence: This is a well-established hypothesis in the literature, cited from Dunbar, 1998.

claim: The ecological brain hypothesis proposes that the increase in brain size and corresponding cognitive skills was driven by the need to build mental representations in order to forage efficiently.
source: Another major theory, referred to as the 'ecological brain' hypothesis, proposes that the increase in brain size and corresponding cognitive skills was driven by the need to build mental representations in order to forage efficiently (Milton, 1981; Milton, 1993).
evidence: This is a well-established hypothesis in the literature, cited from Milton, 1981 and Milton, 1993.

claim: The FP and DLPFC regions were relatively well conserved between humans and macaques in terms of cytoarchitectonics and connectivity profiles.
source: Anatomical studies have shown that these regions were relatively well conserved between humans and macaques, both in terms of cytoarchitectonics and connectivity profiles (Amiez et al., 2019; Petrides et al., 2012; Sallet et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to anatomical studies (Amiez et al., 2019; Petrides et al., 2012; Sallet et al., 2013).

claim: The cognitive functions of FP and DLPFC appear relatively well conserved between macaques and humans.
source: Finally, the cognitive functions in which they are involved appear relatively well conserved between macaques and humans (Ferrucci et al., 2022; Fuster, 2008; Mansouri et al., 2017; Passingham and Sakai, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies demonstrating functional conservation (Ferrucci et al., 2022; Fuster, 2008; Mansouri et al., 2017; Passingham and Sakai, 2004).

claim: The study measured FP volume in 31 brains from 16 primate species.
source: We measured the volume of the FP in 31 brains from 16 species.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the sample size used in the study.

claim: The study measured DLPFC volume in 31 brains from 16 primate species.
source: We measured the volume of the DLPFC in 31 brains from 16 species.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the sample size used in the study.

claim: All brain measures (whole brain, FP, and DLPFC volumes) were highly correlated with correlation coefficient r=0.99.
source: As expected, all these measures were highly correlated (all r=0.99, Pearson correlation).
evidence: This is a statistical result from Pearson correlation analysis of the measured brain volumes.

claim: Body mass has a positive influence on whole brain volume with an estimated coefficient of 0.47±0.15.
source: The values of the estimated coefficients are provided in Table 1. These three variables have a positive influence on the volume of the whole brain. Even if all three factors had a significant effect, their influence on the whole brain volume seemed to differ: there was an order of magnitude between the estimated beta (i.e. contribution) of body mass (0.47±0.15) and that of daily traveled distance (0.05±0.01).
evidence: This is a direct result from the PGLS statistical analysis, with specific coefficient values provided.

claim: Daily traveled distance has a positive influence on whole brain volume with an estimated coefficient of 0.05±0.01.
source: The values of the estimated coefficients are provided in Table 1. These three variables have a positive influence on the volume of the whole brain. Even if all three factors had a significant effect, their influence on the whole brain volume seemed to differ: there was an order of magnitude between the estimated beta (i.e. contribution) of body mass (0.47±0.15) and that of daily traveled distance (0.05±0.01).
evidence: This is a direct result from the PGLS statistical analysis, with specific coefficient values provided.

claim: Population density has a positive influence on whole brain volume with an estimated coefficient of 0.007±0.003.
source: There was also an order of magnitude between the estimated beta of daily traveled distance and population density (0.007±0.003).
evidence: This is a direct result from the PGLS statistical analysis, with specific coefficient values provided.

claim: The influence of body mass on whole brain volume remained significant for all models where one species was removed.
source: The influence of body mass was very robust, in that it remained significant for all models where one species was removed.
evidence: This is a result from the leave-one-out validation procedure conducted to assess model robustness.

claim: Daily traveled distance remained significant for all models but one in the leave-one-out procedure for whole brain volume.
source: Daily traveled distance remained significant for all models but one, whereas population density lost significance (p>0.05) for four models where one species was removed, even if in all cases the estimated coefficient remained positive.
evidence: This is a result from the leave-one-out validation procedure conducted to assess model robustness.

claim: Population density lost significance for four models where one species was removed in the whole brain volume analysis.
source: Daily traveled distance remained significant for all models but one, whereas population density lost significance (p>0.05) for four models where one species was removed, even if in all cases the estimated coefficient remained positive.
evidence: This is a result from the leave-one-out validation procedure conducted to assess model robustness.

claim: Daily traveled distance has a positive influence on FP volume with an estimated coefficient of 0.07±0.02.
source: As for the whole brain, the largest effect is body mass (0.69±0.23), then daily traveled distance (0.07±0.02) and population density (0.011±0.004).
evidence: This is a direct result from the PGLS statistical analysis for FP volume, with specific coefficient values provided.

claim: Population density has a positive influence on FP volume with an estimated coefficient of 0.011±0.004.
source: As for the whole brain, the largest effect is body mass (0.69±0.23), then daily traveled distance (0.07±0.02) and population density (0.011±0.004).
evidence: This is a direct result from the PGLS statistical analysis for FP volume, with specific coefficient values provided.

claim: For FP volume, the coefficients for daily traveled distance and population density have the same order of magnitude.
source: By comparison with the whole brain, however, the coefficients for daily traveled distance and population density have the same order of magnitude such that their impact on the volume of the FP seems to be equivalent.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the statistical results comparing effect sizes across variables for FP volume.

claim: Daily traveled distance has a positive influence on DLPFC volume with an estimated coefficient of 0.047±0.01.
source: As for the whole brain and the FP, the largest effect is body mass (0.47±0.18), followed by daily traveled distance (0.047±0.01).
evidence: This is a direct result from the PGLS statistical analysis for DLPFC volume, with specific coefficient values provided.

claim: The influence of population density on DLPFC volume was very small (0.006±0.003) and failed to reach significance (p=0.067).
source: Even if the best model for DLPFC includes population density, its influence was very small (0.006±0.003) and failed to reach significance (p=0.067).
evidence: This is a direct result from the PGLS statistical analysis for DLPFC volume, with specific coefficient values and p-value provided.

claim: The size of a given brain region provides a good proxy of the strength of its influence on behavior.
source: As we and others have done before (within and across species), we assume that the size of a given brain region provides a good proxy of the strength of its influence (through its known cognitive function) on behavior (Barton and Harvey, 2000; DeCasien and Higham, 2019; Louail et al., 2019; Maguire et al., 2000).
evidence: This is a theoretical assumption supported by citations to previous studies (Barton and Harvey, 2000; DeCasien and Higham, 2019; Louail et al., 2019; Maguire et al., 2000).

claim: The size of a brain region provides a reliable estimate of the number of neurons allocated to its function.
source: Indeed, the size of a brain region provides a reliable estimate of the number of neurons allocated to its function, given the known positive relation between number of cortical neurons and cognitive skills in primates (Herculano-Houzel, 2017; Herculano-Houzel, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies establishing the relationship between brain region size and neuron number (Herculano-Houzel, 2017; Herculano-Houzel, 2018).

claim: There is a known positive relation between number of cortical neurons and cognitive skills in primates.
source: Indeed, the size of a brain region provides a reliable estimate of the number of neurons allocated to its function, given the known positive relation between number of cortical neurons and cognitive skills in primates (Herculano-Houzel, 2017; Herculano-Houzel, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies by Herculano-Houzel (2017, 2018) establishing this relationship.

claim: The frontal pole strongly overlaps with Brodmann area 10.
source: Cytoarchitectonic studies indicate that it strongly overlaps with BA 10 (Ongür et al., 2003; Ramnani and Owen, 2004; Semendeferi et al., 2001; Tsujimoto et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to cytoarchitectonic studies (Ongür et al., 2003; Ramnani and Owen, 2004; Semendeferi et al., 2001; Tsujimoto et al., 2011).

claim: The frontal pole receives projections from the temporal superior cortex.
source: Besides cytoarchitectonic landmarks, the FP can also be identified based on connectivity patterns: it receives projections from the temporal superior cortex (Petrides, 2005) and has connections with the superior temporal sulcus (Sallet et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Petrides, 2005, describing connectivity patterns.

claim: The frontal pole has connections with the superior temporal sulcus.
source: Besides cytoarchitectonic landmarks, the FP can also be identified based on connectivity patterns: it receives projections from the temporal superior cortex (Petrides, 2005) and has connections with the superior temporal sulcus (Sallet et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sallet et al., 2013, describing connectivity patterns.

claim: The anterior limit of the FP was defined as the anterior limit of the brain.
source: The anterior limit of the FP was defined as the anterior limit of the brain.
evidence: This is a methodological description of how the FP was anatomically delimited in the study.

claim: The cingulate sulcus represented the posterior limit of the FP.
source: The cingulate sulcus represented the posterior limit.
evidence: This is a methodological description of how the FP was anatomically delimited in the study.

claim: The ventral limit of the FP was set as the dorsal limit of the gyrus rectus.
source: The ventral limit was set as the dorsal limit of the gyrus rectus.
evidence: This is a methodological description of how the FP was anatomically delimited in the study.

claim: The dorsal limit of the FP was defined as the fundus of the superior frontal sulcus in humans and apes.
source: Finally, the dorsal limit was defined as the fundus of the superior frontal sulcus in humans and apes, or the principal sulcus in monkeys.
evidence: This is a methodological description of how the FP was anatomically delimited in the study.

claim: The dorsal limit of the FP was defined as the principal sulcus in monkeys.
source: Finally, the dorsal limit was defined as the fundus of the superior frontal sulcus in humans and apes, or the principal sulcus in monkeys.
evidence: This is a methodological description of how the FP was anatomically delimited in the study.

claim: DLPFC comprises portions of middle frontal gyrus and superior frontal gyrus in great apes.
source: DLPFC comprises portions of middle frontal gyrus and superior frontal gyrus in great apes and lies in and around the principal sulcus in macaques.
evidence: This is a methodological description of how the DLPFC was anatomically delimited in the study.

claim: DLPFC lies in and around the principal sulcus in macaques.
source: DLPFC comprises portions of middle frontal gyrus and superior frontal gyrus in great apes and lies in and around the principal sulcus in macaques.
evidence: This is a methodological description of how the DLPFC was anatomically delimited in the study.

claim: The ventral limit of DLPFC was set as the fundus of the principal sulcus for monkeys.
source: Then, the ventral limit was set as the fundus of the principal sulcus for monkeys, and the frontal inferior sulcus for apes and humans.
evidence: This is a methodological description of how the DLPFC was anatomically delimited in the study.

claim: The ventral limit of DLPFC was set as the frontal inferior sulcus for apes and humans.
source: Then, the ventral limit was set as the fundus of the principal sulcus for monkeys, and the frontal inferior sulcus for apes and humans.
evidence: This is a methodological description of how the DLPFC was anatomically delimited in the study.

claim: The anterior limit of the DLPFC was defined as the posterior limit of the FP, which was the cingulate sulcus.
source: The anterior limit of the DLPFC was defined as the posterior limit of the FP, which was the cingulate sulcus.
evidence: This is a methodological description of how the DLPFC was anatomically delimited in the study.

claim: For apes and humans, the posterior limit of DLPFC was defined as the precentral sulcus.
source: For apes and humans, the posterior limit was defined as the precentral sulcus, whereas in monkeys it was defined as the end of the arcuate sulcus.
evidence: This is a methodological description of how the DLPFC was anatomically delimited in the study.

claim: In monkeys, the posterior limit of DLPFC was defined as the end of the arcuate sulcus.
source: For apes and humans, the posterior limit was defined as the precentral sulcus, whereas in monkeys it was defined as the end of the arcuate sulcus.
evidence: This is a methodological description of how the DLPFC was anatomically delimited in the study.

claim: The medial limit of DLPFC was designated as the inter-hemispheric sulcus.
source: Finally, the medial limit was designated as the inter-hemispheric sulcus.
evidence: This is a methodological description of how the DLPFC was anatomically delimited in the study.

claim: Eleven socio-ecological variables were selected for the analyses.
source: Eleven socio-ecological variables were selected for the analyses, gathered in different categories: body condition (body mass), diet (dietary quality index and tool use), movements and ranging behavior (daily traveled distance), social parameters (group size, population density, social system), and variables related to reproduction and life-history traits (mating system, mate guarding, seasonal breeding, and weaning age).
evidence: This is a methodological description of the variables included in the study.

claim: The dietary quality index (DQI) was calculated from the formula DQI = 1s+2r+3.5a, where s is the percentage of plant structural parts in the diet, r the percentage of plant reproductive parts, and a the percentage of animal preys.
source: The dietary quality index (DQI) was used to characterize the richness of the dietary spectrum and was calculated from the formula DQI = 1s+2r+3.5a, where s is the percentage of plant structural parts in the diet, r the percentage of plant reproductive parts, and a the percentage of animal preys (Sailer et al., 1985).
evidence: This is a methodological description citing the formula from Sailer et al., 1985.

claim: A low dietary quality index (around 100) characterizes folivorous diets.
source: Thereby, a low index (around 100) characterizes folivorous diets, while a high index (around 200) characterizes more diversified diets (including animals and fruits).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the dietary quality index values based on the formula.

claim: A high dietary quality index (around 200) characterizes more diversified diets including animals and fruits.
source: Thereby, a low index (around 100) characterizes folivorous diets, while a high index (around 200) characterizes more diversified diets (including animals and fruits).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the dietary quality index values based on the formula.

claim: The phylogenetic tree was obtained from the 10ktrees website version 3.
source: The phylogenetic tree was obtained from the 10ktrees website (https://10ktrees.nunn-lab.org/Primates/downloadTrees.php, version 3).
evidence: This is a methodological description of the source of phylogenetic data.

claim: The 10ktrees version 3 provides a Bayesian inference of the primate phylogeny based on collected data for 11 mitochondrial and 6 autosomal genes from GenBank across 301 primate species.
source: This version (Arnold et al., 2010) provides a Bayesian inference of the primate phylogeny based on collected data for 11 mitochondrial and 6 autosomal genes from GenBank across 301 primate species.
evidence: This is a description of the phylogenetic database cited from Arnold et al., 2010.

claim: Brain measurements and body mass were log10-transformed before analyses.
source: Brain measurements and body mass were log10-transformed before analyses.
evidence: This is a methodological description of data preprocessing.

claim: The study used phylogenetic generalized least squares (PGLS) to evaluate the joint influence of socio-ecological variables on neuro-anatomical variability across species.
source: We used a PGLS approach to evaluate the joint influence of socio-ecological variables on the neuro-anatomical variability across species (Grafen, 1989).
evidence: This is a methodological description of the statistical approach used, citing Grafen, 1989.

claim: The PGLS approach allowed the study to take into account the phylogenetic relation across species when evaluating the influence of socio-ecological variables on their neuroanatomy.
source: This approach allowed us to take into account the phylogenetic relation across species when evaluating the influence of socio-ecological variables on their neuroanatomy.
evidence: This is an explanation of the purpose of using PGLS methodology.

claim: The cerebellum was excluded from all brain measurements because it was missing on some of the MRI scans.
source: The cerebellum was excluded from all brain measurements, because it was missing on some of the MRI scans (gorilla brains).
evidence: This is a methodological decision explained by data availability constraints.

claim: Metacognition and working memory are critical for foraging in primates.
source: The strong influence of ecological constraints on FP and DLPFC volumes suggests that both metacognition and working memory are critical for foraging in primates.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the finding that daily traveled distance (ecological constraint) strongly influences FP and DLPFC volumes.

claim: FP is implicated in complex social interactions.
source: Interestingly, FP volume was much more sensitive to social constraints than DLPFC volume, in line with laboratory studies showing an implication of FP in complex social interactions.
evidence: This is supported by the data showing greater sensitivity of FP to population density and by reference to laboratory studies.

claim: The social brain network exists in macaques.
source: Imaging studies in humans have identified a network of brain regions involved in social interactions, and this network is often referred to as the social brain (Stanley and Adolphs, 2013). Recent comparative studies have shown that it also existed in macaques (Rushworth et al., 2013; Sallet et al., 2011; Testard et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to comparative studies (Rushworth et al., 2013; Sallet et al., 2011; Testard et al., 2022).

claim: Specific brain regions (e.g. cingulate cortex) underlie foraging in humans and macaques.
source: Along the same lines, laboratory studies have proposed that specific brain regions (e.g. cingulate cortex) were underlying foraging in humans and macaques (e.g. Hayden et al., 2011; Kolling et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to laboratory studies (Hayden et al., 2011; Kolling et al., 2012).

claim: Social interactions involve categorization of facial expressions and metacognition.
source: For example, social interactions involve some form of categorization of facial expressions and metacognition, and the brain regions associated with these elementary cognitive operations (e.g. frontal pole or temporo-parietal junction) are usually part of the 'social brain', i.e., the set of brain regions associated with social interactions (de Gelder, 2023; de Gelder and Poyo Solanas, 2021; Deen et al., 2023; Devaine et al., 2017; Gallagher and Frith, 2003; Rushworth et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on social cognition (de Gelder, 2023; de Gelder and Poyo Solanas, 2021; Deen et al., 2023; Devaine et al., 2017; Gallagher and Frith, 2003; Rushworth et al., 2013).

claim: Foraging requires spatio-temporal mental representations of food availability and values.
source: Along the same lines, foraging is thought to require spatio-temporal mental representations of food availability and values, and these elementary cognitive operations rely upon a distinct set of brain regions, including the hippocampus and the ventromedial prefrontal cortex (VMPFC) (Lin et al., 2015; Louail et al., 2019; Rosati, 2017; Vikbladh et al., 2019; Zuberbühler and Janmaat, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on foraging cognition (Lin et al., 2015; Louail et al., 2019; Rosati, 2017; Vikbladh et al., 2019; Zuberbühler and Janmaat, 2010).

claim: The brain systems potentially involved in social cognition and foraging partially overlap, especially in the frontal lobes.
source: Finally, the brain systems potentially involved in social cognition and foraging partially overlap, especially in the frontal lobes (Barbey et al., 2014; Gallagher and Frith, 2003; Kolling et al., 2012; Mansouri et al., 2017; Rudebeck et al., 2006; Yoshida et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies showing overlap in brain systems (Barbey et al., 2014; Gallagher and Frith, 2003; Kolling et al., 2012; Mansouri et al., 2017; Rudebeck et al., 2006; Yoshida et al., 2012).

claim: Executive functions allow organisms to organize behavior over space and time to reach a goal.
source: This is typically the case for executive functions (e.g. working memory), which allow to organize behavior over space and time to reach a goal, and rely upon several regions of the prefrontal cortex (Fuster, 2008; Luria, 1973).
evidence: This is a definition of executive functions supported by citations (Fuster, 2008; Luria, 1973).

claim: Executive functions rely upon several regions of the prefrontal cortex.
source: This is typically the case for executive functions (e.g. working memory), which allow to organize behavior over space and time to reach a goal, and rely upon several regions of the prefrontal cortex (Fuster, 2008; Luria, 1973).
evidence: This is supported by citations to foundational work on executive functions (Fuster, 2008; Luria, 1973).

claim: Group hunting only occurs in a few primate species where metacognition is thought to be particularly developed.
source: For example, group hunting, which involves both social and foraging functions, only occurs in a few primate species where metacognition is thought to be particularly developed (Boesch, 1994; Conard et al., 2020; Garcia et al., 2021; Schaik, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on group hunting and cognition (Boesch, 1994; Conard et al., 2020; Garcia et al., 2021; Schaik, 2016).

claim: DLPFC is rarely associated with social interactions in laboratory studies.
source: Its potential relation with social interactions, however, was less clear: on one hand, DLPFC is rarely associated with social interactions in laboratory studies (Frith, 2007; Fuster, 2008; Passingham et al., 2012; Sallet et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to laboratory studies (Frith, 2007; Fuster, 2008; Passingham et al., 2012; Sallet et al., 2013).

claim: Working memory and planning could be involved in complex social interactions in natural conditions.
source: But, on the other hand, working memory and planning could readily be involved in complex social interactions in more natural conditions.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential cognitive involvement in natural behaviors.

claim: There is a positive relation between the size of a given brain region and the relative importance of its associated function, both within and across species.
source: Based on the known positive relation between the size of a given brain region (or the number of corresponding neurons) and the relative importance of its associated function, both within and across species, we assume that the size of each brain region can be taken as a proxy for the weight of its associated function on behavior (Barks et al., 2015; Barton and Harvey, 2000; DeCasien and Higham, 2019; Ferrucci et al., 2022; Herculano-Houzel, 2017; Herculano-Houzel et al., 2016; Louail et al., 2019; Maguire et al., 2000; Sallet et al., 2011; Testard et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by extensive citations to studies establishing this relationship (Barks et al., 2015; Barton and Harvey, 2000; DeCasien and Higham, 2019; Ferrucci et al., 2022; Herculano-Houzel, 2017; Herculano-Houzel et al., 2016; Louail et al., 2019; Maguire et al., 2000; Sallet et al., 2011; Testard et al., 2022).

claim: The FP and DLPFC regions were chosen and identified based on functional maps and reliable macroscopic landmarks rather than cytoarchitectonic criteria.
source: Here, these two regions were chosen and identified based on functional maps and reliable macroscopic landmarks, rather than cytoarchitectonic criteria, to maximize the reliability of the comparative approach (see also Louail et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a methodological decision explained in the text and supported by reference to a previous study (Louail et al., 2019).

claim: The 16 primate species were chosen to cover a wide range of phylogenetic distances coupled to a diversity of socio-ecological variables.
source: The 16 primate species were chosen to cover a wide range of phylogenetic distances coupled to a diversity of socio-ecological variables.
evidence: This is a description of the sampling strategy used in the study.

claim: Differences in regional volume across species provide a reliable index of the differences in neuronal count.
source: Thus, for a given functional region, the differences in regional volume across species provide a reliable index of the differences in neuronal count, and therefore of the skill level in the corresponding function.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known relationship between brain volume and neuron number.

claim: Scaling procedures would distort the relation between volume and neural counts.
source: Even though comparative studies often used scaled measures (i.e. relative to the whole brain) to account for potential allometric effects, we favored absolute measures because scaling procedures would distort the relation between volume and neural counts (Barton et al., 1995; DeCasien et al., 2022; Gabi et al., 2016; Herculano-Houzel, 2017; Herculano-Houzel et al., 2008; Krebs et al., 1989; Smaers et al., 2017; Smaers and Soligo, 2013).
evidence: This is a methodological justification supported by citations (Barton et al., 1995; DeCasien et al., 2022; Gabi et al., 2016; Herculano-Houzel, 2017; Herculano-Houzel et al., 2008; Krebs et al., 1989; Smaers et al., 2017; Smaers and Soligo, 2013).

claim: The volume of the whole brain across primates is positively modulated by body mass as well as social (population density) and ecological (daily traveled distance) variables.
source: In summary, this analysis indicates that the volume of the whole brain across primates is positively modulated by body mass, as well as social (population density) and ecological (daily traveled distance) variables.
evidence: This is a summary of the statistical findings from the PGLS analysis.

claim: The weight of the ecological variable (daily traveled distance) seems to be slightly stronger and more reliable than the weight of the social variable (population density) for whole brain volume.
source: The weight of the ecological variable, however, seems to be slightly stronger and more reliable than the weight of the social variable.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the comparative effect sizes and robustness from the statistical analysis.

claim: Including the whole brain volume as a covariate in the regression models canceled the effects of all other variables for FP volume.
source: Note that, as expected given the strong correlation between FP and whole brain volumes, including the whole brain volume as a covariate in the regression models canceled the effects of all other variables, such that only whole brain showed a significant effect.
evidence: This is a result from the statistical analysis showing the effect of including whole brain as a covariate.

claim: For FP volume, the impact of daily traveled distance and population density seems to be equivalent.
source: By comparison with the whole brain, however, the coefficients for daily traveled distance and population density have the same order of magnitude such that their impact on the volume of the FP seems to be equivalent.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the statistical results comparing effect sizes for FP volume.

claim: The volume of the FP across primates is positively modulated by body mass as well as by both population density and daily traveled distance.
source: Altogether, these data indicate that the volume of the FP across primates is positively modulated by body mass as well as by both population density and daily traveled distance, in line with the idea that it is affected by both social and ecological components.
evidence: This is a summary of the statistical findings from the PGLS analysis for FP volume.

claim: The relative influence of social (population density) and ecological (daily traveled distance) variables are more balanced for FP compared to the whole brain.
source: By comparison with the whole brain, the relative influence of the social (population density) and ecological (daily traveled distance) variables are more balanced.
evidence: This is an interpretation comparing the effect sizes across brain measures.

claim: Including the whole brain volume as a covariate in the regression models canceled the effects of all other variables for DLPFC volume.
source: As it was the case for the FP, including the whole brain volume as a covariate in the regression models canceled the effects of all other variables, such that only whole brain showed a significant effect.
evidence: This is a result from the statistical analysis showing the effect of including whole brain as a covariate.

claim: The volume of the DLPFC across primates is positively modulated by body mass as well as by both ecological (daily traveled distance) and social (population density) variables.
source: In summary, the volume of the DLPFC across primates is also positively modulated by body mass as well as by both ecological (daily traveled distance) and social (population density) variables, but the influence of the later appears much weaker than that of the former.
evidence: This is a summary of the statistical findings from the PGLS analysis for DLPFC volume.

claim: The influence of population density on DLPFC volume appears much weaker than that of daily traveled distance.
source: In summary, the volume of the DLPFC across primates is also positively modulated by body mass as well as by both ecological (daily traveled distance) and social (population density) variables, but the influence of the later appears much weaker than that of the former.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the comparative effect sizes from the statistical analysis.

claim: All three cerebral measures (whole brain, FP, DLPFC) strongly correlated and were influenced by the same set of socio-ecological variables: body mass, daily traveled distance, and population density.
source: Altogether, our results showed that all three cerebral measures strongly correlated and were influenced by the same set of socio-ecological variables: body mass, daily traveled distance, and population density.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from the statistical analyses.

claim: Body mass had a strong and reliable influence on all brain measures.
source: As expected from evidence suggesting brain-body covariation (Martin, 1981), body mass had a strong and reliable influence on all brain measures.
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by reference to previous work on brain-body covariation (Martin, 1981).

claim: Daily traveled distance had a clear positive influence on all brain measures.
source: Daily traveled distance, a proxy for how challenging is foraging, also had a clear positive influence on all brain measures.
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analyses.

claim: Population density was the variable showing the greatest difference in effect size across brain regions.
source: Finally, population density, a proxy for how challenging and complex are social interactions, was generally less powerful at explaining neuro-anatomical variability, but it was also the variable showing the greatest difference in effect size across brain regions.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the comparative effect sizes across different brain regions.

claim: For the FP, the influence of population density was similar to that of daily traveled distance.
source: For the FP, the influence of population density was similar to that of daily traveled distance, but it was much weaker for the whole brain, and it even failed to reach significance for the DLPFC.
evidence: This is a finding from comparing effect sizes across brain regions.

claim: The influence of population density was much weaker for the whole brain compared to FP.
source: For the FP, the influence of population density was similar to that of daily traveled distance, but it was much weaker for the whole brain, and it even failed to reach significance for the DLPFC.
evidence: This is a finding from comparing effect sizes across brain regions.

claim: The influence of population density failed to reach significance for the DLPFC.
source: For the FP, the influence of population density was similar to that of daily traveled distance, but it was much weaker for the whole brain, and it even failed to reach significance for the DLPFC.
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis of DLPFC volume.

claim: The data are generally compatible with the idea that the evolution of executive functions relying upon FP and DLPFC is driven both by ecological and by social constraints.
source: Thus, our data are generally compatible with the idea that the evolution of executive functions relying upon FP and DLPFC is driven both by ecological and by social constraints.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of evolutionary theory.

claim: The relative influence of ecological and social constraints seems to vary across brain regions.
source: Critically, the relative influence of these constraints seems to vary across regions, in line with our hypothesis based on the cognitive functions with which they are associated in laboratory conditions.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the differential effects observed across brain regions.

claim: Neuro-cognitive entities as defined in laboratory conditions can be articulated with socio-ecological processes in the wild to better understand primate cognition and behavior in natural conditions.
source: Thus, neuro-cognitive entities as defined in laboratory conditions can readily be articulated with socio-ecological processes in the wild, in order to better understand primate cognition and behavior in natural conditions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the successful integration of laboratory-based neurocognitive concepts with field-based socio-ecological data.

claim: The stronger sensitivity of the FP to population density is reminiscent of the social brain hypothesis.
source: The stronger sensitivity of the FP to the variable 'population density' is reminiscent of the social brain hypothesis, i.e., the idea that social challenges favored the evolution of larger brains, and especially larger neocortex size, with species living in larger groups having bigger brains to deal with the associated complex social interactions (Dunbar, 1998).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in relation to the social brain hypothesis, citing Dunbar, 1998.

claim: The size of the FP is related to both population density (proxy for social interactions) and daily traveled distance (proxy for foraging complexity).
source: Critically, the size of the FP and the corresponding development of metacognitive skills is not exclusively related to population density (proxy for social interactions) but also to daily traveled distance (proxy for foraging complexity).
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis showing dual influences on FP volume.

claim: The data are compatible with the ecological brain hypothesis.
source: Thus, these data are also compatible with the ecological brain hypothesis (Milton, 1981).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in relation to the ecological brain hypothesis, citing Milton, 1981.

claim: In the wild, social and ecological constraints remain strongly related.
source: This dual relation between FP size, social, and ecological constraints might be accounted for by the fact that in the wild, social and ecological constraints remain strongly related, even if we did not find strong correlations between those factors in our data set.
evidence: This is a general observation about the interconnection of social and ecological factors in natural environments.

claim: Greater population density implies a greater inter-individual competition for food.
source: Indeed, greater population density implies a greater inter-individual competition for food, and thus potentially increases in daily traveled distances, and/or the development of sophisticated foraging skills to deal with the increase in scramble competition.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the relationship between population density and foraging competition.

claim: The benefits associated with increased FP volume could be related to both social and ecological functions.
source: But from a cognitive point of view, this also implies that the benefits associated with increased FP volume, and presumably an increase in metacognitive skills, could be related to both social and ecological functions.
evidence: This is an inference about the functional implications of FP volume increases.

claim: The development of executive functions could have been a critical leverage to allow the development of both complex social interactions and complex foraging.
source: Indeed, as pointed out earlier, the development of executive functions in general, and metacognitive skills in particular, could have been a critical leverage to allow the development of both complex social interactions (through the use of theory of mind) and complex foraging (through flexible, context-dependent planning) (Garcia et al., 2021; Shultz and Dunbar, 2022).
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation supported by citations (Garcia et al., 2021; Shultz and Dunbar, 2022).

claim: The notions of 'social brain' and 'ecological brain' should not be mutually exclusive, even when considering specific brain regions.
source: Thus, our work indicates that the notions of 'social brain' and 'ecological brain' should not be mutually exclusive, even when considering specific brain regions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the finding that both social and ecological variables influence brain regions.

claim: The FP belongs to both the social brain and the ecological brain.
source: Rather, we confirm intuitions based on laboratory studies that the FP, through its role in metacognition, belongs to both sets of brain regions defined as the social brain and the ecological brain, respectively.
evidence: This is a conclusion integrating laboratory findings with the current comparative data.

claim: The size of the DLPFC showed a significant relation with daily traveled distance.
source: The size of the DLPFC, which we used as a proxy for working memory and planning skills, showed a significant relation with daily traveled distance (proxy for foraging complexity), and to a lesser extent with population density (proxy for social complexity).
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis of DLPFC volume.

claim: Working memory and planning are critical for foraging in primates, especially when they need to travel long distances.
source: This suggests that the cognitive functions at play in the DLPFC, i.e., working memory and planning, are critical for foraging in primates, especially when they need to travel long distances, and presumably have to deal with more complex navigation strategies.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the finding that daily traveled distance significantly predicts DLPFC volume.

claim: The finding that DLPFC is related to foraging is in line with the ecological brain hypothesis.
source: This is clearly in line with the global idea of the ecological brain hypothesis, but here we provide a critical insight into the specific neuro-cognitive operations associated with foraging strategies.
evidence: This is an interpretation connecting the findings to the ecological brain hypothesis.

claim: Social interactions seem to rely much more upon rostro-medial prefrontal regions compared to DLPFC.
source: But it is in line with laboratory data showing that social interactions seem to rely much more upon rostro-medial prefrontal regions compared to DLPFC (Fleming and Dolan, 2012; Frith, 2007; Sallet et al., 2011; Testard et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to laboratory studies (Fleming and Dolan, 2012; Frith, 2007; Sallet et al., 2011; Testard et al., 2022).

claim: The work confirms the specificity of the 'social brain' as a set of structures specifically involved in social interactions.
source: In other words, this work confirms the specificity of the 'social brain' as defined in laboratory conditions as a set of structures specifically involved in social interactions (Frith, 2007; Rushworth et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a conclusion supported by the differential effects of social variables on different brain regions and by citations (Frith, 2007; Rushworth et al., 2013).

claim: The results can be integrated in the general framework of the primate mosaic brain evolution.
source: This new set of results can be integrated in the general framework of the primate mosaic brain evolution, i.e., the different distinct structures varying in size both within and between species, and reflecting selection for cognitive skills.
evidence: This is an interpretation placing the findings within the broader theoretical framework of mosaic brain evolution.

claim: The relation between ecology, neurobiology, and cognition can be better captured with more specific brain measures and more specific cognitive operations than by using the cruder measure of brain size.
source: In line with recently published papers (DeCasien et al., 2022; Smaers et al., 2021; van Schaik et al., 2021), we argue that the relation between ecology, neurobiology, and cognition can be better captured with more specific brain measures, and more specific cognitive operations, than by using the cruder measure of brain size.
evidence: This is an argument supported by citations to recent literature (DeCasien et al., 2022; Smaers et al., 2021; van Schaik et al., 2021).

claim: A previous study on VMPFC showed that its size was predicted by a distinct set of ecological variables (dietary quality and weaning age), with little modulation by group size.
source: As it was the case here, VMPFC and whole brain volumes were strongly correlated (r=0.99), but the size of the VMPFC was predicted by a distinct set of ecological variables (dietary quality and weaning age), with little modulation by group size.
evidence: This is a reference to findings from a previous study by the authors on VMPFC.

claim: Specific neuro-cognitive entities can be related to specific socio-ecological challenges that animals face in natural conditions.
source: Thus, our results from these two combined studies suggest that specific neuro-cognitive entities, established in laboratory studies and defined by a conjunction of specific brain regions and cognitive operations, can be related to specific socio-ecological challenges that animals face in natural conditions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from integrating the current study with previous work.

claim: The results confirm that the size of specific brain regions can be related to socio-ecological variables through the cognitive operations relying on these regions in laboratory conditions.
source: In conclusion, our results confirm that the size of specific brain regions can be related to socio-ecological variables through the cognitive operations relying on these regions in laboratory conditions.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the study's main finding.

claim: The approach of articulating cognitive operations reported in laboratory settings with real socio-ecological challenges should provide insight into the neuro-cognitive operations at play in the wild.
source: Thus, our approach which aims at articulating cognitive operations reported in laboratory settings with real socio-ecological challenges should provide a clear insight into the neuro-cognitive operations at play in the wild, as well as their evolution in primates.
evidence: This is a statement about the value and implications of the study's methodological approach.

claim: Integrating realistic socio-ecological challenges can provide insight into the evolution of specific brain functions in primates.
source: Conversely, integrating realistic socio-ecological challenges can provide a strong insight into the evolution of specific brain functions in primates.
evidence: This is a statement about the broader implications of the study's approach.

claim: Thirty-one brain MRI 3D reconstructions from 16 primate species were used in this study.
source: Thirty-one brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) 3D reconstructions from 16 primate species (Ateles fusciceps, n=1; Cebus capucinus, n=1; Cercopithecus mitis, n=1; Gorilla gorilla, n=5; Gorilla beringei, n=1; H. sapiens, n=4; Hylobates lar, n=1; Lagothrix lagotricha, n=1; Lophocebus albigena, n=1; Macaca fascicularis, n=1; Macaca fuscata, n=4; Macaca mulatta, n=2; Pan troglodytes, n=5; Pan paniscus, n=1; Papio papio, n=1, Pongo pygmaeus, n=1) were used in this study.
evidence: This is a description of the sample used in the study.

claim: Brain measurements were processed using Avizo v9.0 software.
source: Brain measurements (visualization, segmentation, and quantification of brain tissues volumes) were processed using Avizo v9.0 software.
evidence: This is a methodological description of the software used for analysis.

claim: Whole brain segmentation was performed using the semi-automated tool in Avizo.
source: Whole brain segmentation was performed using the semi-automated tool in Avizo that enables to select a material or structure according to a specific gray-level threshold.
evidence: This is a methodological description of the segmentation procedure.

claim: Segmentations of the FP and the DLPFC were carried out manually with the brush tool, slice by slice of the MRI scan.
source: Segmentations of the FP and the DLPFC were carried out manually with the brush tool, slice by slice of the MRI scan.
evidence: This is a methodological description of the segmentation procedure.

claim: Each socio-ecological variable was assessed based on the literature on wild populations, whenever possible.
source: Each variable was assessed based on the literature on wild populations, whenever possible, which was the case in a vast majority of cases (and otherwise specified, see below).
evidence: This is a methodological description of how socio-ecological data were collected.

claim: For group size and population density of H. sapiens, an average was taken between industrialized societies and hunter-gatherers societies.
source: For group size and population density of H. sapiens, we took an average between industrialized societies and hunter-gatherers societies.
evidence: This is a methodological description of how human socio-ecological data were estimated.

claim: The effects of captivity and sex on brain measurements were neglected because they were shown to be very small compared to inter-species differences.
source: Thus, we neglected the effects of captivity and sex on brain/endocranium measurements, which were both shown to be very small compared to inter-species differences (Isler and van Schaik, 2012).
evidence: This is a methodological decision justified by citation to Isler and van Schaik, 2012.

claim: Intra-specific variability at the level of the brain was shown to be negligible compared to inter-specific variability.
source: Note, there is also a significant amount of intra-specific variability at the level of the brain, both in humans and in non-human primates, but this intra-specific variability was shown to be negligible compared to inter-specific variability (DeCasien and Higham, 2019; Louail et al., 2019; Maguire et al., 2000; Testard et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies showing the relative magnitude of intra- versus inter-specific variability (DeCasien and Higham, 2019; Louail et al., 2019; Maguire et al., 2000; Testard et al., 2022).

claim: There is no reason to exclude humans from the analysis.
source: We see no reason to exclude humans (as done in previous studies, e.g. DeCasien and Higham, 2019), because even if the brain of H. sapiens is much bigger than others, a general biological law describing the relation between socio-ecology and the brain in primates should also apply to humans (Gabi et al., 2016; Herculano-Houzel, 2017).
evidence: This is a methodological justification supported by citations (Gabi et al., 2016; Herculano-Houzel, 2017).

claim: The global organization of the frontal cortex appears qualitatively similar in humans and other primates.
source: Moreover, even if the human brain is much bigger than that of other primates, the global organization of the frontal cortex appears qualitatively similar in humans and other primates (Barrett et al., 2020; Gabi et al., 2016; Gabi et al., 2016; Roumazeilles et al., 2020; Sallet et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to comparative neuroanatomical studies (Barrett et al., 2020; Gabi et al., 2016; Roumazeilles et al., 2020; Sallet et al., 2013).
